items.title: Jon's Arm Reference, a searchable site for the AArch64 instruction set and system registers, closes on December 4, 2026 at Arm's request; a reference a project depends on is safest taken from the vendor's own published source
items.summary: Jon's Arm Reference (arm.jonpalmisc.com) gives searchable documentation for the AArch64 instructions (base, SIMD, SVE and SME) and the AArch64 and AArch32 system registers of the Armv8-A and Armv9-A architectures. Its author announces that it will close on December 4, 2026, after Arm's lawyers asked for it to be taken down, and that he is looking for a way to keep its links working. The site states no licence and no data source.

notice.developer: A third-party reference built from a vendor's documentation can disappear at the vendor's request. Link the vendor's own pages in code and documents, and save the version you used.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's machines run on x86-64 and arm64 hosts, and its tools cite architecture references. Citing the vendor's own published source, with its version, keeps a citation valid when a convenient mirror closes.

items.title: Micro language models of 8 to 30 million parameters write the first four to eight words of an answer on the device in 55 ms while a cloud model continues it; people rated the joined answer as good as the cloud's alone or better in 75.6% of judgments
items.summary: Wen Cheng, Tuochao Chen, Karim Helwani, Sriram Srinivasan, Luke Zettlemoyer and Shyamnath Gollakota, of the University of Washington and Meta AI, present micro language models at EMNLP 2026 (pages 3240-3264). Models of 8.8 to 29.5 million parameters, trained from scratch on 1.485 billion tokens of chat, write the first 4 to 8 words of an answer on the device and commit them; a cloud model, prompted as a continuator, finishes the sentence. On an Orange Pi the 28M model gives its first token in 45 ms and four words in 55 ms, against 0.2 to 5 seconds or more for a cloud answer. The cloud model must correct the opener in 3.7% of answers at 4 words, 8.4% at 8 and 16.4% at 16. With 25 participants the joined answer was preferred in 33.6% of cases, judged equal in 42.0% and the cloud's alone preferred in 24.4%; in a live test 10 participants preferred it in 42 of 50 trials. The checkpoint and a demo are published. The figures are the authors' own.

notice.developer: The wait before the first word is what a user feels. A model small enough for a watch can write the first words while a large model answers the rest; keep the committed opener to 4 to 8 words, where the large model rarely has to repair it.
notice.maintainer: Softanza places models where the data and the user are. This paper adds a placement: a micro model on the device for the first words, a large model for the rest, joined mid-sentence. It sets a figure to measure Softanza's own small models against, the time to the first word on the user's machine.
notice.learner: A very small AI on your watch can start an answer at once while a big AI far away writes the rest, so you never wait for the first word.

actions.do: measure the time to the first word of the local answer path on the client's machine beside the time to the whole answer, and evaluate a micro opener model that writes the first 4 to 8 words while the chosen model continues, counting how often the continuation must repair the opener

sources.title: Micro Language Models Enable Instant Responses
sources.by: Wen Cheng, Tuochao Chen, Karim Helwani, Sriram Srinivasan, Luke Zettlemoyer, Shyamnath Gollakota

items.title: open486 rebuilds a 486 PC in one FPGA, with its own microcoded core, x87 unit, graphics, sound and BIOS, and runs Windows 95, DOOM and Quake on one FPGA board after two weeks of work
items.summary: open486, a Vayner Systems project begun on November 12, 2026, rebuilds a 486-compatible PC in a Digilent Arty A7-100T FPGA at 50 MHz: its own staged, microcoded CPU core with an x87 unit, its own SVGA, Sound Blaster 16, OPL3 and MPU-401 audio, NE2000 network, IDE on microSD, and its own BIOS and VGA BIOS, using about 59,000 of the board's 63,400 LUTs (93%). It runs DOS and Windows 95 OSR2.5, browses the web from Windows 95, and runs DOOM, Quake, Wolfenstein 3D and Prince of Persia. It scores 174 on TopBench in CrystalMark Retro 2.1.0. Cycle counts are published per instruction against Intel's 486 manual. The source is to be published under Apache 2.0. The figures are the project's own.

notice.developer: A whole PC, processor to sound card, fits in one mid-range FPGA, and its makers publish cycle counts per instruction against the original manual: a model of how to show a hardware design's progress.
notice.learner: Someone rebuilt a 1990s computer chip out of a reprogrammable chip, and it runs Windows 95 and DOOM.

items.title: OpenAI and Cisco publish Shirudo, a BSD-licensed runtime that loads signed eBPF patches into a running Linux system to block an exploit until the fix ships, each load verified by the kernel and recorded in the TPM
items.summary: On November 23, 2026 OpenAI and Cisco introduced Shirudo, an open-source runtime (BSD 2-Clause, its BPF programs dual BSD and GPL) that protects a running Linux system while a patch is prepared. A protection, called an upatch, is a signed eBPF loader that attaches to hooks such as BPF LSM, fentry and fexit, uprobes and XDP; the kernel checks its ML-DSA-87 signature against a sealed keyring before it loads, and every change to the loaded set extends a TPM 2.0 register that can be attested offline. Engineers and agents can write upatches. In a controlled test, a Codex-generated protection added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and blocked an exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch without a restart. The project is pre-release and needs a kernel with its signed-loader patches. The claims are the vendors' own.

notice.developer: A flaw can be blocked in a running service before its fix ships: a small signed program in the kernel checks the input the exploit needs. It is a mitigation for the days between the advisory and the patch, and its signature and its record in the TPM say which ones ran.
notice.maintainer: Harobanda declares its machine and pins its kernel; between two pins, an advisory waits. Shirudo shows a signed, attested way to cover that wait with a narrow program loaded live, and an agent that writes it. Its requirement, a patched kernel with a sealed keyring, is the price to weigh against the next pin.

actions.do: for the next advisory that reaches a pinned kernel or a service in a Harobanda machine, write down the days between the advisory and the pin that fixes it, and evaluate on one machine whether a signed eBPF mitigation in Shirudo's shape, with its load recorded, covers those days

items.title: Together AI distils Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao translation into Qwen3.8-27B for $260 in all, from 4,000 teacher translations, reaching 93% of the teacher's score while a language it was not trained on holds
items.summary: Together AI (Zain Hasan and Sonny Khan, November 26, 2026) taught Qwen3.8-27B to translate English into Lao from Kimi-K3.1-Pro's own translations. The two models use different tokenizers, so the teacher passes only text: it translates FLORES-200 and Wikipedia sentences at temperature 0 with thinking off, a filter keeps translations written at least 70% in the target script, and the student is trained on them with LoRA and cross-entropy on its own chat template. On chrF++ the student's Lao rises from 5.5 to 44.3, against 47.5 for the teacher, and its Thai, mixed into the data, rises from 46.7 to 47.8; training on 945 human Lao references alone scores 44.7 on Lao and drops Thai to 5.3. The teacher's 4,000 Lao translations cost $7.46 and all the experiments $260. A five-language adapter raised Northern Sotho from 32.7 to 48.0 and Zulu from 37.7 to 39.2. The figures are the authors' own.

notice.learner: A large AI model can teach a small one a new language from its own translations; check the languages the small one already knew, because it can forget them.
notice.developer: A large model's translations can teach a small one a language it barely knows, for a few dollars of teacher text. Check a language you did not train on as well: training on Lao alone took the student's Thai from 46.7 to 5.3.
notice.maintainer: Softanza measures its models language by language, and runs small models where the data lives. This recipe moves a large model's skill in one language into a small model, with text alone, across different tokenizers: the way to raise a language where the local model trails, measured with a guard language beside it.

actions.do: for each language of the matrix where a small local model trails a large one, generate the large model's translations of public sentences, keep those in the right script, train the small model on them with a guard language mixed in, and measure on held-out sentences the target language, the guard language, and the cost of the teacher's text

sources.title: Distilling Kimi into Qwen
sources.by: Zain Hasan and Sonny Khan, Together AI

items.title: llm.asm runs Qwen3-0.6B from 17,252 lines of x86-64 assembly, as a 14.7 KB Linux program with no libc and as a 24 KB kernel booted by GRUB; it states decode speeds above llama.cpp's on the same processor
items.summary: llm.asm (MIT, published by alesha-pro on November 25, 2026) runs the full 28-layer forward pass of Qwen3-0.6B, with its BPE tokenizer, in NASM assembly. It comes as a static Linux program of 14,712 bytes that uses raw system calls and no libc, and as a bare-metal kernel of 24,252 bytes booted by GRUB through Multiboot, with VGA text, a PS/2 keyboard and a serial port, which boots in 74 to 94 ms. A Python script converts the published weights once into a 613.66 MiB Q8_0 file. On an AMD EPYC 7642 the author measures 20.70 tokens per second on one thread and 125.86 on 40, and states 18 to 36% faster decoding than llama.cpp at Q8_0, with the prompt read one token at a time where llama.cpp reads it in batches; the kernel reaches 134.9 tokens per second under KVM. Its greedy output matches PyTorch on 64 of 64 tokens. The figures are the author's own.

notice.developer: A small model needs very little beneath it: a forward pass, a tokenizer, threads and memory. The program around the weights can be kilobytes; the weights themselves stay hundreds of megabytes, and a speed comparison holds only when both sides read the prompt the same way.
notice.maintainer: Harobanda declares the machine an application runs on. llm.asm shows how small that machine can be when its one job is a 0.6B model: 24 KB of kernel, under a tenth of a second to boot. That is a floor Harobanda can measure its own image against.

actions.do: take llm.asm's figures as the floor for a machine that only runs a small model: build a Harobanda image that runs Qwen3-0.6B at Q8_0 and measure, on the same virtual machine, its image size without the weights, its time from boot to the first token, and its decode speed at 1 and at every core, beside llm.asm's kernel

sources.title: Tiny assembly LLM runs without Linux or libraries

items.title: MeMo trains a small model on question-answer pairs drawn from a corpus and lets the main model question it in place of a search index; it leads retrieval on long narratives and ties it on web questions, at 240 to 420 GPU-hours per corpus
items.summary: MeMo: Memory as a Model (arXiv 2605.15156, May 2026), by nine authors from NUS, A*STAR, the University of Tokyo, Liquid AI, MIT CSAIL and the Singapore-MIT Alliance, replaces the retrieval index with a model. A 32B generator turns the corpus into question-answer pairs (about 0.7 to 1.6 million per corpus); a smaller model, Qwen2.5-14B in the main setting, is fully fine-tuned on them and never sees the documents; the main model, left unchanged, questions it in three stages. On NarrativeQA with Gemini 3 Flash as the main model, MeMo scores 53.58% against 26.62% for dense retrieval and 23.21% for graph retrieval; on BrowseComp-Plus graph retrieval scores 56.11% against MeMo's 54.22% with Qwen2.5-32B, and the two tie with Gemini. With added false documents, retrieval loses up to 6.22 points and MeMo stays level. Building one corpus's memory costs about 240 to 420 H200 GPU-hours. The figures are the authors' own.

notice.developer: Retrieval finds the passages that look like the question; an answer spread across a long story or many documents is where it falls short. A model trained on the corpus can hold those connections, at the price of training it, and of training it again when the documents change.
notice.maintainer: Softanza runs small models on the machine that holds the data. MeMo's memory model is that kind of model, specialised to one corpus. Its cost of 240 to 420 GPU-hours per corpus and its update by model merging decide where it fits: a fixed corpus, many cross-document questions, and a client who keeps the data at home.

actions.do: record MeMo in the needs map as a candidate for a fixed corpus whose questions span many documents, with its cost per corpus; and when a client corpus of that kind exists, measure a small memory model trained on its question-answer pairs against retrieval with the same main model, counting accuracy, hours to build, and hours to absorb a changed document

sources.title: MeMo: Memory as a Model
sources.by: Ryan Wei Heng Quek, Sanghyuk Lee, Alfred Wei Lun Leong, Arun Verma, Alok Prakash, Nancy F. Chen, Bryan Kian Hsiang Low, Daniela Rus, Armando Solar-Lezama

items.title: Declare, a user-interface language written by models and checked by its compiler: half React's lines and eleven hidden checks of eleven in one run; Softanza measures Zayn and Haro's diagnostics the same way
items.summary: Declare, by David Temkin (co-founder of Laszlo Systems, which made OpenLaszlo), is an MIT-licensed declarative language for user interfaces, described as a UI language for you and your AI. Square brackets hold the view tree and braces hold TypeScript; an attribute in braces is a constraint whose dependencies the compiler extracts, and an assignment makes its dependents recompute. There is no CSS. The same tree renders to the DOM, to a canvas or to a native Mac host, in Node or the browser with no build step. It ships an agent skill, a six-rung verifier, and diagnostics that each name the rewrite that fixes them. In the author's single-run comparison, a ticket-buying app took 1,279 lines against React's 2,666, and its first build that ran passed eleven hidden checks of eleven against React's six. The figures are the author's own.

notice.developer: Code a model writes is usually judged by whether it looks right. A language whose structure the compiler can check, and whose every error names its fix, lets the model correct itself before a person reads the result.
notice.maintainer: Softanza has its own interface (Zayn) and its own language (Haro), both meant to be written by models. Declare measures what that buys: lines, compiler errors per build, and hidden checks passed by the first build that runs. The same three figures apply to a Zayn screen, and a diagnostic that names its fix is a form Haro can count.

actions.do: give a model one small Zayn application to build under hidden behaviour checks, as Declare's ticket-buying test does, and record the lines written, the compiler errors per build, and the checks passed by the first build that runs
count, over a sample of agent sessions, the share of Haro's diagnostics that name the rewrite that fixes them, and give that form to the most frequent ones

items.title: Besimple post-trains two open speech models on medical terms for about $500 and beats three closed models on medical dictation; Softanza measures its own transcriber on the words of a domain
items.summary: On November 23, 2026 Baseten published how Besimple adapted two open speech recognition models, Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Qwen3-ASR, to medical vocabulary. From a dictionary of 274,541 terms they generated sentences, spoke them with synthetic voices of varied accents, replaced about 29% of those clips with human recordings over several rounds, and mixed in general speech: 813 hours in all, trained with LoRA for an estimated $500 of GPU time for both models. Errors on medical terms in human dictation fell from 2.83% to 0.87% for Nemotron and from 5.84% to 2.05% for Qwen3-ASR; the best closed model measured scored 1.05%. On general English speech the adapted models stay behind the closed ones, and Qwen3-ASR lost ground there. The figures are the authors' own.

notice.developer: An overall word error rate hides the words that matter. A transcriber can be right on 95% of words and wrong on the drug name; score the domain's terms on their own, and keep a general set to see what adapting cost.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's transcriber runs Whisper in its own engine, raises its hearing with a glossary prompt, and already routes Hausa to an adapted checkpoint by the court's measure. The same route serves a domain: a term-dense set spoken from the glossary, errors on terms scored apart, and an adapter kept only where it wins.

actions.do: score the transcriber's errors on a domain's own words apart from its overall word error rate, on a term-dense set spoken from the glossary and a general set kept as a guard against regression; then compare the glossary prompt with a small adapter trained on that set, and route a domain to the adapter only where the court measures it better

sources.title: Post-train your own medical ASR model to outperform the frontier
sources.by: Lei Pan, Ardin Lo, Brandon Tai, Reese Tateo, Yi Zhong (Baseten, Besimple)

items.title: Microsoft announces seven MAI models at Ignite, among them a coding model priced against GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 and a routing model built on Gemma 4; Softanza states the price basis of every comparison and measures its own router
items.summary: At Ignite on November 17, 2026, Microsoft AI announced seven models: MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash for coding, MAI Cyber 2 Flash for security defence, MAI Image 2.7 and MAI Image 2.7 Flash, MAI Realtime 1 for live speech to speech, and Microsoft Decision 1.1 for routing requests inside applications. Microsoft states that MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's at 5%, averaged over four coding benchmarks, with MAI Code 2's cost taken at its 50% promotional price. MAI Realtime 1 is priced at $0.01 per audio minute. Decision 1.1 is built on Gemma 4 26B A4B and is described as 50 times faster and 79 times cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. The coding models are in GitHub Copilot; none of the seven is released as open weights. The figures are Microsoft's own.

notice.developer: A model priced at a fraction of another is a claim about two things: the score and the price. Microsoft's 5% of Claude Opus 5.5's cost uses MAI Code 2's promotional price, half its list price; read the footnote before the headline.
notice.maintainer: A large lab now sells a routing model, built on an open model, as a product of its own. Softanza routes with its court, by measured results per task. The court's own figures as a router, cost per decision and cost per correct answer, are the comparison this release invites.

actions.do: measure the court's choice of model on the bench as a router: its cost per decision, the share of tasks where it picks the model that scores best, and the cost per correct answer against always running the single best model; and state in every published cost comparison whether the price is a list price

sources.title: Seven new world-class models at scalable price-performance
Introducing MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash
MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash in GitHub Copilot

items.title: Anthropic interviews 58 companies: AI's value comes from more output and from roles rebuilt around a whole workflow, and the bottleneck is review; Softanza's Foundry states the review each pack creates
items.summary: On November 23, 2026 Anthropic's economics team (Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory) published Working with AI, a study of 66 face-to-face interviews in 58 US companies adopting AI, covering nearly 300 applications. Most of the value interviewees reported came from more output rather than lower cost, and around half of the output gains came from doing existing work faster. The largest gains came with broad change: one person or team owning a whole workflow, and staff moved to the tasks that hold work up. The bottlenecks named were inside the companies, above all the load of reviewing what AI produces and uneven adoption. Two-thirds of the companies reported hiring less because of AI, 10 reported hiring more, and two saw a position fully automated away. The authors describe the study as qualitative, with value as the interviewees describe it.

notice.developer: When AI writes more, a person reviews more. The study found that review, not the model, is where work most often waits, so the time a reviewer spends per item is the figure that decides whether a tool pays.
notice.maintainer: A Softanza pack delivers an agentic solution whole. The study says the value of such a solution shows as output and as a role rebuilt around the workflow, and that review is the common bottleneck; each pack can state the review it creates and its measured minutes per item.

actions.do: record in each pack's delivery the review its outputs need: what a person checks, how many items a day, and the minutes per item measured in the pilot; and report the pack's value as the output it adds, beside any cost it removes

sources.title: Working with AI
sources.by: Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)

items.title: Google gives Agent Substrate 1.0 and gVisor to the CNCF: an agent holds no credential, and the gateway adds it outside the sandbox; Softanza reads its credential broker against that line
items.summary: On November 5, 2026 Google Cloud announced the donation of Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, with Agent Substrate at version 1.0 under Apache-2.0. Each agent session, called an actor, runs in its own gVisor sandbox or Cloud Hypervisor microVM on Kubernetes, with its own files, memory and network rules; plain Linux containers are refused. Networking is deny by default, and an actor holds no API key or cloud token: an egress gateway outside the sandbox adds the credential to each approved outbound request. An idle actor is snapshotted and its slot freed; the project reports a resume in under 500 ms and more than 500 activations per second. The figures are the project's own.

notice.developer: The safest place for a secret is outside the process that could be tricked. An agent that never holds its credential cannot leak it: a gateway it cannot change adds the credential to the requests a policy approved.
notice.maintainer: Softanza brokers a credential by name inside the agent's process. Agent Substrate draws the line one step further out, at the outbound request, and Softanza's own boundary outside the process is the place to state which side each guarantee stands on.

actions.do: state in the threat model which guarantees of the credential broker hold when the agent's own process is hostile, and measure one governed outbound call whose credential is added by a process outside the agent, so that the agent's memory never holds it

sources.title: Sandboxing untrusted AI agents at scale

items.title: OpenAI describes the sandbox of its coding agent: rules by the operating system, a tool server outside them by default, and deny patterns read once at start; Softanza checks its own rules at each access
items.summary: On November 18, 2026 OpenAI published an engineering account of the sandbox in Codex, its coding agent. Shell commands run under the operating system's own mechanisms: Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap with seccomp-bpf on Linux, and a Microsoft sandbox on Windows. The built-in workspace profile allows writes inside the workspace, keeps the .git and .codex folders read-only, and closes the network; an optional proxy applies allow and deny rules by domain. The article states three bounds in its own words: a tool server started over standard input and output runs outside the sandbox by default, deny patterns are expanded when the sandbox starts so a file created later is outside them, and name lookups can carry data out.

notice.developer: A rule expanded once protects the files that existed at that moment. A file created afterwards is a new name, so a rule that must hold is decided each time a file is opened.
notice.maintainer: Softanza decides a path or a command at the moment an agent asks for it. OpenAI's account names two places worth a guard of their own: a forbidden file created after the rules load, and a tool server started for an agent, which should run inside the agent's bounds.

actions.do: add a guard that creates a forbidden file after the rules are loaded and shows the agent is refused it, and run a tool server started for an agent under the same file and network bounds as the agent, with one measured call

items.title: A small on-device agent that decided correctly several times is more likely to allow what its policy forbids; Softanza's governed actor decides each act apart from the model
items.summary: In 'Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents' (arXiv 2611.27216, November 20, 2026) Chong Tian and co-authors study small agents that run on a device and hand some work to a cloud model under restrictions. They find that correct earlier decisions in a session make a later violation more likely, an effect they name correct-precedent generalization: in 13 open-weight models from nine developers, and a single correct precedent can roughly halve the safe rate of the most affected agent. Their remedy, Paired Decision Distillation, trains a small adapter on the decisions of a weakly affected teacher and restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, with no added prompt text or model call. The abstract was read; the figures are the authors'.

notice.developer: A small model's decision depends on the session before it: after a few allowed requests it tends to allow the next one too. A restriction that must hold is checked by code that sees the single act, with no history.
notice.maintainer: Softanza lets a small model propose and a governed actor decide, so a forbidden act is refused whatever the session held. The paper gives a precise test for the models of the court: the refusal rate after one, three and five correct allowed decisions.

actions.do: measure on the court's small models the rate at which a forbidden act is refused after zero, one, three and five correct allowed decisions in the same session, and show with a guard that the governed actor refuses the act in every case

sources.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents

items.title: A study of four coding agents finds that a rules file is advice and a gate is a decision: agents crossed a written boundary in 7 of 45 runs without a gate; Softanza gives each rule that matters a gate
items.summary: In 'Markdown Is Not a Firewall' (arXiv 2611.27112, November 20, 2026) Sandeep Dhuri gives one 278-word rules file to four coding agents, Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode, on 20 small repositories with hidden tests and four planted boundaries: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. With no gate in front of the forbidden service, 7 of 45 runs reached it. Behind a gate that blocks and logs, agents tried to cross a boundary in 5 of 90 steps. The file also had a cost: one agent's hidden-test pass rate fell from 99.0% to 67.7% with it, and in 11 of its 36 steps it reported completion while under half the tests passed. The abstract was read; the figures are the author's.

notice.developer: A file tells an agent what you want, and a gate decides what it gets. Write the rule for the agent to read, and put a check in code in front of every act that must never happen.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's desks work under written rules, and its secret check before a commit is a rule with a gate. The study gives the reason to list the written rules that guard an irreversible act and give each one a check that refuses in code.

actions.do: list the rules in the desks' instruction files that guard an irreversible or outward act, and give each a gate that refuses in code, as the secret check before a commit already does; count the rules with a gate and the rules that are text only

sources.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries

items.title: Small open models asked to quote the page that proves each answer reach 84.5% on company filings, and 16 to 167 wrong answers in 1,000 pass every automatic check; Softanza counts the same on its own set
items.summary: In 'Show Your Work' (arXiv 2611.24990, November 18, 2026) Krishna Nandula publishes Filing-Evidence: 1,000 questions over 90 annual and quarterly filings of 45 United States companies, with answer keys taken from the filings' own machine-readable tags. Each answer must give a page and a verbatim quote, which a program checks. Ten open models of 7 to 21 billion parameters ran on one RTX 4090. Accuracy with checkable evidence ran from 17.1% to 82.7% in the plain setup, and the best result was 84.5%, by Qwen3.5-9B. Between 16 and 167 answers per 1,000 were wrong and passed every automatic check; 57% of those were errors of scale or unit. Retrying after a failed check added up to 3.9 points. Code and data are public. The abstract was read; the figures are the author's.

notice.developer: Ask a model for the quote and the place that prove its answer, and check both by program. Then count the answers that pass the check and are wrong: that number is the true limit of the check, and here most of them were a thousand or a million read as a unit.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's model court judges small models on a golden set. The paper adds a measure the court can take on its extraction tasks: answers with a quote a program verified, and among them the wrong answers the check let through, by kind.

actions.do: ask each extraction answer of the support-desk set for a verbatim quote and its place in the source, verify both by program, and report per model the answers that pass the check and are wrong, sorted by kind of error

sources.title: Show Your Work: Can Small Open Models Read SEC Filings with Evidence a Machine Can Check?

items.title: GPUOS runs background work beside a latency-bound model on one GPU by making it yield at checkpoints; Softanza learns the yield rule for its own GPU jobs
items.summary: GPUOS is an MIT research prototype from the Multi-V-VM group, described as sharing a GPU without NVIDIA's MIG or MPS. Its code keeps one persistent kernel running on the GPU with a work queue, replaces operators at run time through a table of device function pointers, and merges many tiny operations into one compiled batch. Its working-draft paper, pushed on November 12, 2026, builds on OpenInfer's 'The GPU Needs an Operating System' and specifies restartable tasks admitted under revocable resource leases. On one RTX 5090, background work that yields every 4 tiles costs a streaming foreground 0.62% at the 99th percentile, against 23.68% when it never yields. The authors state that the measurements support selected mechanisms.

notice.developer: Background work on a GPU is safe beside a latency-bound job when it is cut into short slices and checks, between slices, whether the foreground wants the device. The size of the slice is the price: GPUOS measured 0.62% of foreground cost with a short slice and 23.68% with none.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's engine gives the GPU one owner at a time across processes. Inside that owner, the same rule applies one level down: a background job dispatches in short slices and yields to a foreground job between them, with the foreground's 99th-percentile time measured both ways.

actions.do: inside the process that holds the GPU, let a background job dispatch in short slices and yield to a foreground job between them; measure the foreground's median and 99th-percentile step time alone, beside a background job that never yields and beside one that yields, with the background's own rate in each case; and measure the engine's fixed cost per dispatch, which says when merging small operations into one dispatch pays

sources.title: GPUOS: An Operating-System Architecture for Shared GPU Execution (working draft, source in the repository)

items.title: Tur serves eight requests from one small model at six times the speed of one by reading the weights once per step; Softanza measures the same rule on its own decoder
items.summary: Tur, by Danylo Kravchenko, is an Apache-2.0 inference engine in Rust for Apple Silicon Macs: one binary for generation, an OpenAI-compatible server, Whisper transcription and quantization, on Metal kernels and the Candle framework. Its continuous batching packs every request's next token into one pass, so the weights are read once for all of them: on an M3 Pro, Qwen3.5-0.8B at 8 bits decodes 123 tokens per second for one sequence and 729 for eight, against llama.cpp's 113 and 456. It plans all memory before loading a weight, keeps most experts of a mixture-of-experts model on the SSD behind a fixed cache, reuses shared prefixes, and drafts tokens from the prompt's own text. Figures are the author's.

notice.developer: One decode step of a small model is mostly the time to read its weights from memory. Several sequences decoded in the same step share that read, so total speed grows with the number of sequences while each one slows a little: Tur reports a gap between tokens of 17.4 ms alone and 25.9 ms with eight.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's decoder holds several models in slots under one memory budget and decodes one sequence at a time. Decoding several independent sequences of one model in one step is the next measure: total tokens per second at 1, 2, 4 and 8 sequences on the processor, with each sequence's text identical to its solo run.

actions.do: decode several independent sequences of one model in one step and measure total tokens per second and the gap between tokens at 1, 2, 4 and 8 sequences on the processor, each sequence's text identical to its solo run; and measure drafting from the prompt's own text, which adds no second model, on a task that copies from its prompt

sources.title: Tur: local inference with a little muscle

items.title: Google's TPU Sync moves a model's working memory between chip, host memory, disk and network; Softanza manages its small models' state as one memory budget
items.summary: On November 9, 2026 Google Cloud announced TPU Sync, an open-source C++ library with PyTorch and JAX bindings that treats a TPU's on-chip memory, the host's pinned memory, shared storage and the data-centre network as one hierarchy for a model's key-value cache and weights. Tensors keep the chip's own layout at every level and move by direct memory access while the chip computes. In Google's lab test of July 2026 on TPU v7x, serving Qwen3 235B with prefill and decode on separate nodes, the median transfer of the cache fell from several seconds to about 230 ms and time to first token fell by 60% on average; with prefix caching on 64K-token contexts it reports up to 90% lower time to first token.

notice.developer: What a model has already read is an asset: stored in the layout the engine computes on, it can leave fast memory and come back without conversion. Keep it by a hash of the text it stands for, and evict the least recently used first.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's decoder already keeps a read prompt in memory and on disk, keyed by the model's hash; with several small models on one machine it adds the layer above: one memory budget for weights and read prompts, with a measured time to bring each back.

actions.do: measure, for each model of the support-desk set, the time from disk to first token with a cold file, a file already in the system's cache and a restored prefix cache, and the memory each holds when ready; then give the engine one memory budget across loaded models and their prefix caches, evicting the least recently used to disk, and report how many models stay ready within the budget

sources.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU

items.title: llmgw puts one gateway in front of an organisation's own GPUs; Softanza learns its priority bands and its residency rule
items.summary: llmgw, by Ilker Manap, is a gateway in one Go binary for organisations that run language models on their own GPU clusters: one OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoint over vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and TensorRT-LLM, with tenants, keys, budgets, guardrails, per-tenant knowledge bases and a three-machine high-availability setup. Its README, at version 0.16.3 of November 3, 2026, reports that the gateway adds 0.15 to 0.49 ms at the 99th percentile with authentication and guardrail patterns on, measured on loopback, and that with admission control interactive latency stays within 1.24 times idle while 500 batch requests run, against 58 times without. It is published under the Functional Source License, which becomes Apache 2.0 after two years.

notice.developer: When people and background jobs share one model, give each request a priority band and let the low band wait: llmgw reports interactive answers within 1.24 times their idle latency under 500 batch requests, and 58 times without that rule.
notice.maintainer: Softanza runs its agents and models on the user's own machine, where several agents share one local model; it takes from llmgw two declared rules: a person's request is admitted ahead of background work, and a project marked as resident refuses any model outside, as a fallback too.

actions.do: declare a priority band for each agent that calls a model, admit a person-facing call ahead of background calls when several agents share one local model, and measure a person's answer time with background agents running, with and without the rule; declare where a solution's model calls may run, refuse a model outside that place as a fallback too, and write the refusal in the run's record

items.title: NVIDIA FLARE 2.9.1 admits a site to shared training only after its hardware and software match what all parties approved; Softanza's federation learns the admission rule
items.summary: NVIDIA FLARE 2.9.1, released on November 12, 2026 under Apache-2.0, adds confidential computing as an optional technical preview to its federated-learning framework. Training runs inside confidential virtual machines or confidential containers on Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP, with or without NVIDIA confidential GPUs, on a site's own servers, on Kubernetes or on Azure, all in one federation. The application's image, code, configuration and secrets sit in an encrypted vault whose key the Trustee key broker releases only after the machine's measured boot matches approved reference values. Sites then check each other's evidence at registration and periodically; a site that fails is refused or quarantined.

notice.developer: Two decisions protect a shared computation: the key that opens the workload is released only to a machine whose measurements match an approved list, and each participant checks the others' evidence when they join and again while they run. A valid proof says which code runs; it says nothing about whether that code is safe.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's compute federation admits a host by name, endpoint and facets, then governs, signs and encrypts each call. The admission rule adds what the host runs: its engine build and model hashes compared with a list every party approved, checked at joining and on a period, with each refusal written to the security ledger.

actions.do: give the compute federation an admission rule: a joining host presents a signed statement of the engine build and model hashes it runs, the federation compares it with an approved reference list, repeats the check on a period, retires a host whose statement stops matching, and writes each refusal to the security ledger; state in the rule's own text that a statement is declared by the host and that hardware evidence is the stronger form

sources.title: Release 2.9.1: Confidential computing and security enhancements

items.title: OpenInfer measures a serving GPU's math units busy 6 to 11% of the time and schedules the rest; Softanza gives its one GPU a single owner
items.summary: In 'The GPU Needs an Operating System' (arXiv 2611.08720, November 5, 2026), Reza Nourai and Behnam Bastani of OpenInfer measure two large open models served with stock vLLM on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell cards: the tensor units are active 6 to 11% of the time while kernels occupy the GPU about 94% of it, because each decoding step waits on memory. They propose a scheduler that lends idle parts of the chip to background work in pieces of 20 microseconds or less. With NVIDIA's static partitions, work written to share adds about a quarter of a GPU at a 5% slower decode step; their research kernel, running Llama-3.1-8B, adds the same at 0.3 to 1.6%.

notice.developer: A GPU that reports itself busy can have most of its arithmetic idle: text generation is limited by how fast memory delivers the weights. Read tokens per second and memory bandwidth, and treat the utilisation percentage as occupancy.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's GPU faculty already reports each kernel against the measured arithmetic peak and the memory bandwidth of the adapter; the paper adds the question of who may use the GPU at a given moment, and Softanza answers it for one machine with one owner at a time.

actions.do: give the GPU one owner at a time across processes: a named lease the engine takes before it creates its device, so that a second process waits its turn or runs its job on the CPU; and report, for one decode step of a court model, the fraction of the adapter's measured peak and of its memory bandwidth

sources.title: The GPU Needs an Operating System (arXiv 2611.08720v1)
Busy isn't efficient: why the GPU needs an operating system

items.title: llama.cpp and ggml reach version 1.0.0 with a versioning promise; Softanza moves its engine's ggml to the stable line
items.summary: On November 13, 2026 the ggml-org team at Hugging Face released llama.cpp v1.0.0 and ggml v1.0.0, three and a half years after the project began. Both libraries now follow semantic versioning: a breaking change to the public C API in their include folders raises the major version, a compatible feature, backend update or new model raises the minor, a bug fix raises the patch. To get there, llama.h loses 35 deprecated functions and ggml loses its deprecated API and the legacy DIAG_MASK operations. The release also adds FP8 key-value caches, an unbuffered model load on Windows, three text architectures, and fixes in llama-server for SSRF, CORS and DNS rebinding.

notice.developer: From 1.0.0 the version number of llama.cpp and ggml tells you what an upgrade costs: only a new major version changes the C API your application calls. If you run llama-server on a network, take this release for its SSRF, CORS and DNS-rebinding fixes.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's engine builds its own decoder directly on ggml, vendored at 0.29.0 from nine days earlier; it moves to 1.0.0, the first version whose number carries a compatibility promise, and keeps its neural checks as the proof.

actions.do: move the engine's vendored ggml from 0.29.0 to tag v1.0.0 with the same pruning and patches, list every ggml function the engine calls against the 1.0.0 headers, run the neural, OCR and vision checks and the court's golden sets on both builds, and record 1.x as the line the engine follows

sources.title: llama.cpp v1.0.0: A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

items.title: A small recogniser trained on synthetic Arabic words reads words it never saw; Softanza trains its Arabic recogniser the same way
items.summary: An engineer reports fine-tuning Microsoft's TrOCR-Small, a 61-million-parameter recogniser of single printed text lines trained on English receipts, into an Arabic word reader: 78,000 unique Arabic words rendered into about 900,000 synthetic images with realistic augmentation, 80 minutes on one RTX 3090, 97.6% exact-word accuracy on vocabulary held out of training and 77.3% on photographs of street signs. TrOCR pairs an image Transformer encoder with a text Transformer decoder, scores 95.86 F1 on SROIE in its small size, and reads one line at a time.

notice.developer: A recogniser learns a script from rendered text: tens of thousands of words, many fonts, realistic damage, and a test on words kept out of training; one consumer GPU and about an hour were enough for Arabic.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's OCR already runs an Arabic recogniser in its own engine; it trains that recogniser on synthetic lines built from its Arabic word list, with the periods and Western digits real documents carry, and judges it on its Arabic golden sentences.

actions.do: generate synthetic Arabic text lines from the engine's Arabic word list, with punctuation, Western and Arabic-Indic digits and mixed Latin words, in several fonts with scan and photo damage; fine-tune the PP-OCR Arabic recogniser the engine already runs on them, test on words held out of training, and judge it on the Arabic golden sentences against the platform floor

sources.title: TrOCR: Transformer-based Optical Character Recognition with Pre-trained Models

items.title: NVIDIA SkillSpector scans an agent skill before it is installed; Softanza checks its agent files the same way
items.summary: NVIDIA SkillSpector is an open-source (Apache 2.0) scanner for the skills that coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI install, at v2.13.4 on November 4, 2026. It checks a skill from a directory, a file, a zip, a URL or a Git repository against 71 patterns in 17 categories, among them prompt injection, data exfiltration, excessive agency, memory poisoning and MCP tool poisoning, first by static analysis and optionally by a language model, and reports a 0-100 risk score in terminal, JSON, Markdown or SARIF. Its README cites a study of 31,132 marketplace skills in which 26.1% held at least one vulnerability and 5.2% showed likely malicious intent.

notice.developer: A skill your coding agent installs runs with its trust; scan it first with SkillSpector's static mode, which needs no model and no key.
notice.maintainer: A Softanza agent file is data that may come from a colleague or a model; Softanza checks its text for the same risks SkillSpector names, and Radar shows the scan before any install it suggests.

actions.do: check a .pia agent file at load for the risks SkillSpector names that apply to it (instructions that override the agent's role, endpoints that could carry data out, tools beyond the declared task, MCP servers with broader rights than needed), reported in the unified rule shape through stzRuleReport beside the existing function and posture refusals
show a SkillSpector static scan before every skill install a Radar lesson suggests

items.title: Rayline's ARC: an open 0.8B model that picks the model for each step of an agent; Softanza learns its local-first escalation
items.summary: On November 11, 2026 Rayline Labs announced ARC 1.0, an open-weight (Apache 2.0) routing model built on Qwen3.5-0.8B. For each step of an agent it predicts, per candidate model, the probability of success and the tokens the step will bill, then a policy weighs that success against the prices the application supplies; a question head answers developer-defined yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities. On six benchmarks Rayline reports that ARC, routing between Opus 5.5 and a locally served DeepSeek model, keeps 97.5% of Opus 5.5's quality at 92.9% lower cost.

notice.developer: A small model can decide which model answers each step: ARC predicts success and cost per candidate, and its prefer-local policy keeps a step on your own machine whenever the local model is predicted to succeed.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's court picks one local model per task from evidence; ARC shows the per-call layer above it, and Softanza measures escalating from a 1B model to a larger local pack only when the small model's own option probability is low.

actions.do: measure local escalation on the support-desk golden sets: Granite-4.0-1b answers by StzOptionProbabilities, and a question whose top option probability falls below a threshold goes to the support-quality pack; first check on the same sets that the top probability is calibrated, then record accuracy and seconds per question against each model alone, across thresholds

sources.title: ARC: Learned Model Routing for Long-Horizon Agentic Workflows

items.title: Samsung's LittleBit stores a model's weights in under one bit each; Softanza weighs memory against quality on its small models
items.summary: LittleBit, from Samsung Research (NeurIPS 2025; fifth version February 5, 2026), compresses a language model's weights to between 0.1 and 1 bit per weight by factoring each weight matrix into two low-rank matrices of signs with three scaling vectors, plus a residual path of the same shape, trained against the original model. The paper reports Llama2-13B in under 0.9 GB at 0.1 bits per weight, about 31 times smaller than 16-bit, and a speedup of up to 11.6 times on one layer with its GPU kernel. Its code, with the follow-up LittleBit-2 (ICML 2026), is published under the non-commercial CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.

notice.maintainer: Below one bit per weight, a 13B model fits in under a gigabyte, at a measurable cost in quality; Softanza's own question is how low its small models can go and still win their court hearings.

actions.do: measure Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B in the lowest-bit GGUF formats the engine's ggml reads, against its Q4_K_M file on the support-desk golden sets: memory, CPU speed and court score at each format, to find the smallest file that keeps its triage-extract win

sources.title: LittleBit: Ultra Low-Bit Quantization via Latent Factorization (arXiv 2506.13771v5)
sources.by: Banseok Lee, Dongkyu Kim, Youngcheon You, Youngmin Kim (Samsung Research)

items.title: A2UI 1.0: an open protocol for agents to answer with a native screen; Zane gives it intent and law, and a projection to it
items.summary: On November 11, 2026 the A2UI project, started at Google, released A2UI 1.0 under Apache 2.0: a streaming protocol in which an agent sends a screen as data, built only from components the app registered in a locked catalog, and each app draws it with its own native components in React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI and soon Jetpack Compose. Version 1.0 adds typed function calls in both directions, components from several catalogs on one screen, and A2UI Express, which its authors say describes the same screen in about three times fewer output tokens than JSON. Gemini, Atlassian and ByteDance ship it.

notice.developer: An agent can now answer with a form, a chart or a choice that every app draws natively, sent as data and never as code; A2UI 1.0 is the open protocol for it.
notice.maintainer: Zane declares what the human is doing and checks it against its constitution; an A2UI projection lets a checked Zane declaration reach every A2UI renderer, and an A2UI check lets Zane judge screens other agents send.

actions.do: add an A2UI v1.0 projection: compile a checked Zane declaration into createSurface, updateComponents and updateDataModel messages over a Zane catalog, so a screen the constitution passed renders natively in every A2UI renderer
read an A2UI message stream an agent produced and check it against the constitution's structural rules before it renders, citing rule numbers, as the verifier does for .zane files

measure which screen format a small local model writes validly under the engine's constrained decoding: a Zane declaration, A2UI JSON or A2UI Express, counting valid screens and output tokens with Granite-4.0-1b on a fixed set of requests

items.title: Liquid AI's LFM3: six 2B-class models on one backbone, built for the device; Softanza learns from its decision models
items.summary: On October 27, 2026 Liquid AI released LFM3, six open-weight models of about 2 billion parameters each (text, vision with video, audio with speech output, omni, and two d1 decision models), all branched from one 1.7B base. The base mixes 13 gated short-convolution layers with 5 sliding-window and 6 global attention layers, fits in about 1 GB at 4 bits, reads 256K tokens and covers 16 languages, Arabic and French among them. The d1 models answer a list of questions about one input in a single forward pass, each answer with a calibrated probability.

notice.developer: A 1 GB open model for local agents now reads Arabic and French with a 256K context, and its d1 sibling answers several yes/no, choice and score questions about one input in one pass.
notice.maintainer: Softanza already reads answers by probability, which beat generation on its golden sets; it measures LFM3's d1 shape, many questions over one shared prefill, and weighs the LFM3 decoder family beside Gemma 4.

actions.do: measure answering several option questions over one shared prefill of the same input, the shape of LFM3's d1 models, against one StzOptionProbabilities call per question, on the support-desk golden sets: same answers, fewer prefill tokens

weigh the LFM3 decoder family (gated short convolutions, sliding-window and gated global attention, partial RoPE) beside Gemma 4 for the engine's next decoder port, then put LFM3-1.7B before the model court against Granite-4.0-1b with its speeds recorded

sources.title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

items.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B: a 4 GB model for local agents; Softanza adds its Gemma 4 family and takes it to the model court
items.summary: On October 23, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B, a small language model post-trained by reinforcement learning from Google's Gemma 4 E4B for multi-turn tool use, instruction following and grounding. It has 8 billion parameters, 4 billion of them effective, a 64K-token context, and ships as a 4 GB Q4_K_M GGUF file for llama.cpp with a companion DFlash drafter for speculative decoding. Its weights, training data and recipes are published under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence, and NVIDIA's own benchmark table puts it ahead of Gemma 4 E4B on most of 21 agent and instruction tests.

notice.developer: A 4 GB open model tuned for tool calls and short answers now runs locally through llama.cpp; Softanza tests it on its own golden sets before it offers it.
notice.maintainer: Bolt E4B uses the Gemma 4 architecture, so Softanza's engine adds that decoder family first, then the model court compares Bolt with Granite-4.0-1b on extraction, classification and brief.

actions.do: add the Gemma 4 decoder family (Gemma 4 E4B and its per-layer embeddings) to the engine's own Zig decoder, checked token by token against a reference run of the same GGUF file

put Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B (Q4_K_M) before the model court as a challenger to Granite-4.0-1b on the support-desk golden sets, read by probability as the incumbent is, and record CPU and wgpu speeds on the 6 GB laptop GPU beside the scores

sources.title: NVIDIA's models on Hugging Face, Nemotron 3.5

items.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B finds pages by text or by image in 34 languages; Softanza measures it on Arabic and French retrieval
items.summary: On October 20, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B, an embedding model that turns a query, a passage or the image of a document page into one vector, for retrieval across text, tables, charts and infographics. NVIDIA evaluated text retrieval in 34 languages, Arabic, French and Persian among them, and image retrieval in 18; its vectors can be cut to 1024 or 512 dimensions and stay usable once normalised. It is published under OpenMDW-1.1, with an NVFP4 variant for recent NVIDIA GPUs.

notice.developer: A 1B open model now retrieves document pages from their images as well as their text, in many languages; Softanza keeps its own embedding model until a multilingual test says otherwise.
notice.maintainer: Softanza adds Arabic and French retrieval items to its embedding golden set, so the court can judge multilingual challengers such as Nemotron 3.5 Embed against MiniLM and SigLIP2.

actions.do: add Arabic and French items to the retrieval golden set, so the model court can judge a multilingual embedding challenger against all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on text and SigLIP2 on page images

items.title: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Parse reads a page into text, tables and layout with 0.63 billion parameters; Softanza's OCR court hears it
items.summary: On October 17, 2026 NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a 0.631-billion-parameter model that turns a page image into text, tables, chart data, reading order, semantic classes and bounding boxes, exported as Markdown, HTML or JSON. NVIDIA reports 75.20 on the ParseBench benchmark in its three-pass mode, the best of the systems it compares, and multilingual OCR evaluated over 163 language and script entries. On November 4 it added a native 89.3-million-parameter DFlash2 drafter for speculative decoding; the model is published under OpenMDW-1.1.

notice.developer: An open 0.63B model now reads whole pages, tables and charts included, into Markdown or JSON; Softanza measures it against its own OCR pipeline before choosing.
notice.maintainer: Softanza's OCR court measures Nemotron 3.5 Parse on its golden pages, by a reference run, before any port of its encoder and decoder is planned.

actions.do: run Nemotron 3.5 Parse once by its published reference path on the OCR plane's golden pages, single and triple pass, and enter the result in the OCR court beside the PP-OCR pipeline and Granite-Docling, with the languages and scripts each one reads

items.title: NVIDIA OpenShell governs an agent from outside its process; Softanza adds that boundary to the rules it already decides in code
items.summary: NVIDIA OpenShell is an open-source (Apache 2.0) runtime for AI agents, at v0.1.8 on November 10, 2026, and moving to the CNCF. Each agent runs in a sandbox whose files, system calls and network are confined by the kernel, a supervisor outside the agent checks every outbound request against a deny-by-default policy and adds real credentials only to requests bound for approved endpoints, and a prover uses formal logic to show what new access a policy change would grant before it is applied. It runs on Linux, on macOS with Apple Silicon, and on Windows through WSL 2 or Microsoft MXC.

notice.developer: An agent that never holds a real credential cannot leak it: OpenShell adds the secret only to a request bound for an approved endpoint, outside the agent's reach.
notice.maintainer: Softanza already decides in code which functions an agent may call and under which posture; it adds the boundary OpenShell shows, enforcement outside the agent's process, for secrets first and for model-written code next.

actions.do: broker credentials for agents: an agent's outbound call names a secret held in stzSecretStore, and the engine attaches its value only to a request bound for an endpoint the governance approves, so neither the agent's code nor the model ever holds the value

run model-written code and an agent's child processes inside an operating-system boundary outside the agent's process, deny by default on files and network (on Windows a job object or AppContainer, on Linux namespaces with seccomp or Landlock), and measure what each platform enforces natively

show, before a governance change is accepted, the access it adds: the functions, postures, endpoints and secrets an agent could reach after the change and not before, computed from the rules themselves

items.title: NVIDIA Snapshot restores a warmed-up GPU inference worker in seconds; Softanza saves the warm state it pays for, a read prompt
items.summary: On November 8, 2026 NVIDIA released Snapshot v0.3.0, an open-source (Apache 2.0) Kubernetes system that checkpoints a fully initialised GPU inference pod, CPU and GPU memory together, and restores it on another node instead of starting it again. It combines CRIU for the process with NVIDIA's cuda-checkpoint for the GPU, and works with vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. On NVIDIA's own B200 tests, restore was 8.1 to 35.9 times faster than a cold start across 22 configurations, for example 4.7 seconds against 104 seconds for Qwen3-0.6B on vLLM.

notice.developer: Restoring a warm process beats rebuilding it; for a small local model the warm state worth keeping is the prompt the model has already read, which can be saved and reloaded.
notice.maintainer: Softanza loads a small model in 0.2 to 1.3 seconds, so its cost is reading long fixed prompts; it measures saving a prefilled KV cache and restoring it against prefilling again.

actions.do: save the KV cache of a prefilled fixed prompt (system instructions, examples, a document) to disk, keyed by the model's sha256 and the prompt's tokens, and restore it instead of prefilling; measure restore time against the recorded 38.5 tokens per second CPU prefill, and check the next-token probabilities are identical

sources.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Snapshot: Fast Startup for Inference Workloads on Kubernetes

items.title: NVIDIA ships a small drafter with each new model and speeds up llama.cpp; Softanza takes the algorithm into its own decoder
items.summary: On September 3, 2026 NVIDIA said its work with the llama.cpp and vLLM communities gives up to 1.9 times higher local throughput on a GeForce RTX 5090, from GPU kernel work, better speculative decoding and faster prefill. Since then its new models ship with a small DFlash drafter, which llama.cpp's official server runs, and its open-source C++ runtime TensorRT Edge-LLM (0.11.1, October 28) added the Bolt E4B drafter and TensorRT for RTX on Windows. Most of the speed comes from CUDA code for NVIDIA's newest GPUs; the speculative-decoding algorithm itself is portable.

notice.maintainer: Softanza's decoder keeps its CPU and wgpu paths and measures speculative decoding with a small drafter of the same tokenizer, against its recorded 17.6 tokens per second decode.

actions.do: measure speculative decoding in the engine's Zig decoder (a small drafter proposes several tokens, the main model checks them in one pass), with a drafter that shares the main model's tokenizer, against the recorded Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B decode of 17.6 tokens per second on the CPU
record the upstream ggml commit Softanza's vendored copy came from, so each later ggml improvement can be judged against it

sources.title: Sparks Fly: NVIDIA Accelerates Local AI at IFA 2026
NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB (model card, quick start with the DFlash drafter)

items.title: Radar runs for any project: one file says what its agent learns and watches
items.summary: Radar now reads everything that belongs to its project from one file, radar.yaml: the project, the watch, its readers, its map, and what the watching agent learns before each survey. The feed, the site with its trends, and the bar take their names and texts from it, and version 1.1.0 of the bar reads any watch's feed with the key the page gives it.

notice.developer: Any project can run its own Radar: copy the repository, write radar.yaml, and point the bar at your feed with data-feed and data-key.
notice.maintainer: Radar's project-specific values now live in radar.yaml, checked before every run; bar 1.1.0 is the version to pin, and 1.0.0 keeps working.

items.title: A coding agent's "don't ask again" writes secrets into a file that gets published
items.summary: Apiiro reports that when a Claude Code user approves a command with "Yes, and don't ask again", the exact command, including any password or key typed into it, is saved as a permission rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project. The file is kept out of git only by the developer's global ignore list, not by the repository's own .gitignore, and Apiiro counted 1,122 public copies on GitHub holding a real secret, out of 104,185.

notice.developer: Open .claude/settings.local.json in each project you use a coding agent in, delete any rule that contains a password, key or token, and rotate it if the file was ever committed.
notice.maintainer: Add .claude/settings.local.json to your repository's own .gitignore, and scan agent folders, transcripts and memory files for passwords written inside commands.

actions.do: add .claude/settings.local.json to the repository's own .gitignore, so the protection travels with the repository and not with one machine
add .claude/settings.local.json to the repository's own .gitignore, for the same reason
add a check for passwords written inside commands (PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p, mysql -p, bearer headers) over agent settings, transcripts, memory files and handoff notes
write the house rule: a secret is referenced as an environment variable in a command, never typed into it

sources.title: Coding Agents Copy Your Secrets to a Hidden File. Thousands Are on GitHub

items.title: Radar's feed is signed: check it came from this repository unchanged
items.summary: Radar publishes an SSH signature beside each feed file, feed/index.json.sig and feed/feed.json.sig, made with one Ed25519 key kept for this purpose by Radar's maintainer. Any reader with OpenSSH can check a feed with ssh-keygen against the public key and the namespace radar-feed. The change adds files and adds nothing to the feed itself, so the feed stays at version 1; docs/FEED.md gives the key, its fingerprint and the command.

notice.developer: Radar's feed carries a signature beside each file; a program that shows its notices should check it with ssh-keygen before showing anything.
notice.maintainer: Pin Radar's key fingerprint in your reader rather than fetching the key from the same place as the feed.

actions.do: add the signature check to the reader proposed in docs/READER.md, with the key's fingerprint pinned in the library

items.title: GitHub will block pull_request_target in public repositories from December 2
items.summary: GitHub announced on November 2, 2026 that from December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions blocks pull_request_target events by default in every public repository unless an Actions event policy allows them. Enforcement is tried in two windows, November 9 and November 16, 16:00 to 18:00 UTC. Private and internal repositories are not affected.

notice.developer: If your public project's workflows use pull_request_target, expect them to fail on November 9 and 16 between 16:00 and 18:00 UTC, and to stop from December 2 unless you allow them.
notice.maintainer: Check your public repositories for pull_request_target before December 2; Softanza's own repositories do not use it.

items.title: Code repaired by a model after an API change can pass its checks and still be wrong
items.summary: A study submitted on November 5, 2026 looks at code that models repair after documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Repairs that run cleanly can still give wrong answers: a gate built on typical inputs let 41% of the wrong repairs through, and adding one input written from the release note cut that to 6.5%. The expected outputs came from the old program on the old runtime.

notice.developer: When an agent repairs code for a changed API, test the repair with one input that exercises the change, and take the expected answer from the old version.
notice.learner: A program that runs without errors can still be wrong: test it with the case that changed, not only with the usual ones.
notice.maintainer: Gate every model-made port or repair on edge inputs taken from the change itself, with expected outputs from the old runtime, never from the model's own tests alone.

actions.do: for code ported to Haro by an agent, gate each change on at least one input that exercises the documented difference, with the expected output read off the old runtime

sources.title: Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations

items.title: Radar opens: a public watch on AI, read from Softanza's point of view
items.summary: Softanza opened Radar, a public repository that reads developments in AI at their source and judges each one against what Softanza builds. Every entry is written twice in one file, as a page for people and as data for programs, and a feed is generated from the data.

items.title: Two MCP clients let a malicious server obtain a token meant for another server
items.summary: Two advisories published on November 5, 2026 describe the same flaw in two MCP clients, the Go SDK mcp-go before 1.2.1 and the ChatCLI agent before 1.215.2: the client took the resource named in a server's protected resource metadata without checking that it matched the server it had connected to. A malicious MCP server could name another server on the same authorization server, have the user sign in, and replay the token it received.

notice.developer: If you use mcp-go or ChatCLI, update to mcp-go 1.2.1 or ChatCLI 1.215.2, and only sign in to MCP servers you chose yourself.
notice.maintainer: An MCP client must check that the resource a server declares is the server URL it connected to before it asks for a token.

actions.do: record as a requirement for any MCP client Softanza builds: the declared resource is checked against the configured server URL before a token is requested, with a guard that a mismatching server is refused

sources.title: GHSA-h3x9-8c36-m89w: mcp-go OAuth protected resource metadata not validated
GHSA-2gm2-hpg7-78f2: ChatCLI MCP OAuth resource indicator

items.title: SPILLWAY: an agent may act only on targets that came from a trusted, typed field
items.summary: A paper submitted on November 4, 2026 proposes a defence for tool-using agents against prompt injection that does not rely on a model: a call with side effects is admitted only if every target it names that is not in the user's request was returned in a typed identity field, such as an email address or a channel, by a read-only tool. A rule-based sanitizer removes instruction-like text, and a local model reviews only the calls the rule refused. The authors report no successful in-scope attack across twelve benchmark settings.

notice.developer: A strong defence against prompt injection is a plain rule, not a smarter model: let an agent send or pay only to a target that came from the user or from a trusted, typed field.
notice.maintainer: Compare Softanza's tool governance with SPILLWAY's admission rule: where a side effect's target comes from matters as much as which tool is allowed.

actions.do: study whether Softanza's agent governance can check the provenance of a side effect's target, not only the tool's name, and report what it would take

sources.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection

items.title: A prompt library ran any function a template named: tools must come from a registry
items.summary: The Python prompt library banks, up to version 2.4.2, read a tool's import path from the text of a prompt template and imported and called whatever it named when the model asked for that tool (CVE-2026-61536, high). Whoever could write a template, in a shared registry or a fetched prompt, could run code in the application. Version 2.4.3 resolves tools only from a registry filled at render time.

notice.developer: If your agent resolves a tool from a name or path found in a prompt or a config file, resolve it only against a list of tools you registered in code.
notice.maintainer: Check that every way an agent finds a tool goes through an explicit registry, never through an import or a lookup built from text.

actions.do: check that declarative agents resolve their tools only against tools registered in code, and add a guard that a tool named only in the agent's text is refused

sources.title: GHSA-64vx-6h2c-rjh7: banks CompletionExtension tool import path
The fix: resolve tool callables from an explicit registry
